title: Lumbar decompression surgery | NHS inform
text:
Lumbar decompression surgery
Lumbar decompression surgery aims to improve symptoms that are caused by pressure on the nerves in the lower spine. For example, persistent pain and numbness in the legs.
When lumbar decompression surgery is used
Lumbar decompression surgery may be used to treat:
spinal stenosis – the space around the spinal canal narrows, which puts pressure on the nerves inside
a disc bulge and
sciatica
– a spinal disc presses on a surrounding nerve or nerves
spinal injuries – like a fracture or swollen tissue
cauda equina syndrome
– the nerves in the spinal canal become severely compressed
When is lumbar decompression surgery recommended
Lumbar decompression surgery is only recommended when non-surgical treatments have not helped. Non-surgical treatments include painkillers, physiotherapy and sometimes spinal injections.
It may also be recommended if you experience serious side effects from medication and these affect your ability to work.
Surgery will only be suggested if you’re healthy enough to have a
general anaesthetic
and the surgery. It may only be recommended if your
body mass index (BMI)
is 35 or below.
Types of lumbar decompression surgery
There are different procedures for lumbar decompression surgery. Often, a combination of techniques may be used.
The specific procedure that your surgeon recommends for you will be discussed with you. They’ll also give you an information leaflet relevant to your procedure.
Preparing for lumbar decompression surgery
If you’re going to have lumbar decompression surgery, it helps to be as fit as possible before surgery. For example, you could
exercise regularly
,
eat healthily
and
stop smoking
(if you smoke). This can help to reduce the risk of complications.
Find out more about waiting well
Pre-operative assessment
You’ll have a pre-operative assessment a few days or weeks before your operation.
During this appointment, you may need to have some tests like
blood tests
.
You’ll also have a general health check to make sure you’re fit for surgery.
Lumbar decompression surgery is carried out by a neurosurgeon or a specialist spinal orthopaedic surgeon. You will be told who’ll be doing your operation and have an appointment with them. Often, you’ll also sign a consent form at this appointment so that you know what’s involved and the potential risks.
You can use this appointment to discuss any concerns you have about your surgery. It’s also a good chance to
ask any questions you have.
You could write down any questions you have before your appointment.
Before the operation
You’ll be admitted to hospital either on the day of your operation or the day before. Your surgeon and anaesthetist will explain what will happen during the operation. This will give you another opportunity to ask any questions.
You’ll usually be asked not to eat or drink for about 6 hours before the operation.
What happens during lumbar decompression surgery
The operation is carried out under
general anaesthetic
. This means you’ll be asleep during the procedure. The whole operation takes at least an hour, but it may take much longer, depending on how complex it is.
During lumbar decompression surgery, you’ll lie face down on a special mattress. This allows the surgeon to access the affected part of your spine.
Risks of lumbar decompression surgery
As with any type of surgery, there are risks and complications associated with lumbar decompression surgery. This includes:
damage to the nerve root and the lining that surrounds the nerve roots – can cause back or leg pain, weakness or numbness, leaking from the wound, headaches or, very rarely,
meningitis
recurrence of sciatica due to post operative scar tissue
skin and nerve injuries, and eye problems – these could be due to positioning during surgery, but special mattresses are used to minimise this risk
infection
blood clots in the legs (
deep vein thrombosis)
or lungs (pulmonary embolism)
bleeding
Although rare, the surgery may make your symptoms worse than before.
There are also other very rare but serious complications, including cauda equina and paralysis. This is the loss of use of the legs, loss of sensation and loss of control of the bladder and bowel.
Other risks include a
stroke
,
heart attack
, or other medical or anaesthetic problems, including death. This is reported as happening in 1 out of 250,000 cases under
general anaesthetic
.
Recovering from lumbar decompression surgery
When you wake up after lumbar decompression surgery, your back may feel sore. You may have one or more tubes, including:
a drip to supply fluids into a vein (intravenous drip) – to make sure you don’t get dehydrated
a drain – to take away any fluid from your wound
a thin, flexible tube inserted into your bladder (
urinary catheter
) – in case you have difficulty urinating
The tubes are usually only attached for a short time after your operation.
You’ll also be given painkillers by your healthcare team.
Rehabilitation
Your medical team will get you up and moving as soon as possible, either on the day of the operation or the day after. This is because inactivity can increase your risk of developing
a blood clot in the leg
. Movement can also speed up the recovery process.
After your operation, a physiotherapist will check that you can move safely and take you on stairs to make sure you’re fit for discharge. They’ll teach you some simple exercises you can do at home to help your recovery.
You’ll need to avoid more strenuous activities for 6 weeks or longer. It can take a minimum of 6 weeks for the pain and tiredness after your operation to disappear completely, and sometimes longer.
Going home after surgery
These are general guidelines about going home after surgery. Your recovery will depend on different factors like your age, health and the support you have at home.
You’ll usually be well enough to leave hospital 1 to 4 days after surgery. This will depend on how complex the surgery was. It’ll also depend on your fitness and activity levels before surgery.
When you get home, it’s important to take things easy at first. Gradually increase your level of activity as you feel able. You may need some help at home for at least the first week after surgery.
You may be able to return to work after about 4 to 6 weeks if you work in a job that doesn’t require too much movement. You may need more time off if your job involves driving for long periods or lifting heavy objects. This can be up to 3 months or longer.
It will take a minimum of 6 weeks and sometimes longer to get your full mobility and function back. This will depend on the severity of your condition and symptoms before the operation.
Driving
Before driving again, you should be:
free from the effects of any painkillers that make you drowsy
able to do an emergency stop without pain (you can practice without starting your car)
comfortable in the driving position
Most people feel ready to drive at least 4 to 6 weeks, depending on the size of the operation.
Some insurance companies don’t insure drivers for many weeks after surgery. Contact your insurer for further information.

NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde
